title: Frog Jump
statement:
A frog wants to get across a river by hopping between stones. `stones` lists the stones' positions along the river, in units, sorted in strictly increasing order; the frog starts on the first stone and must never land anywhere that is not a stone.

- Every jump goes forward (toward larger positions).
- The very first jump is exactly 1 unit long.
- After a jump of `k` units, the next jump must be `k - 1`, `k` or `k + 1` units long (and a jump is always at least 1 unit).

Return `true` if some sequence of jumps lets the frog land on the last stone, otherwise `false`.
notes:
## Intuition

Where the frog can go next depends on two things: which stone it stands on and how long its last jump was. That pair is the state. Trying every jump sequence by brute force branches three ways per jump, but many sequences reach the same (stone, jump) pair, so we record each pair once in a table `dp[i][k]`: "the frog can stand on stone `i` after a jump of `k` units". Jump lengths grow by at most 1 per jump, so after reaching stone `j` the last jump is at most `j`, and the table needs only `n + 1` columns.

## Approach

1. Make `dp`, an `n` by `n + 1` table of zeros, and set `dp[0][0] = 1` (standing on the first stone with a "jump of 0", so the next jump is 1).
2. For each stone `i`, look back at earlier stones `j`, nearest first. The jump from `j` is `k = stones[i] - stones[j]`.
3. If `k > j + 1`, no jump from `j` can be that long, and farther stones only make `k` bigger and `j` smaller, so stop looking back.
4. Otherwise the frog can make the jump if it reached `j` with a jump of `k - 1`, `k` or `k + 1`; then set `dp[i][k] = 1`.
5. The answer is whether any entry of the last row is 1.

## Example 1, step by step

`stones = [0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 12, 17]`. Position 1 gets `k = 1` from position 0. Position 3 gets `k = 2` from position 1. Position 5 gets `k = 2` from 3; position 6 gets `k = 3` from 3 and `k = 1` from 5. Position 8 gets `k = 3` from 5 and `k = 2` from 6. Position 12 gets `k = 4` from 8 (which had `k = 3`). Position 17 gets `k = 5` from 12 (which had `k = 4`), so the last row has a 1 and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each stone looks back at most at all earlier stones, with constant work each.
- Space: O(n²): the table has `n · (n + 1)` small entries.

## Pitfalls

- The first jump must be exactly 1: if `stones[1] != 1` the answer is `false`.
- Jumps of length 0 or less are not allowed; the `dp[0][0]` start state only allows a jump of 1.
- Positions reach 2^31 − 1, so index the table by stone index and jump length, never by position.
- Stopping at `k > j + 1` is what keeps the scan short; it is valid only when scanning `j` from nearest to farthest.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of stones |
| `dp[i][k]` | 1 if the frog can be on stone `i` having just jumped `k` units |
| `i` | the stone being reached |
| `j` | the earlier stone the jump starts from |
| `k` | the length of the jump from stone `j` to stone `i` |
